q: A function with items=[] remembers values from earlier calls. Explain and repair it.
a: Default arguments are evaluated when the function is defined. Use None and allocate a list per call.
explanation: A caller-supplied list still has its own mutation semantics. Decide whether to mutate it or copy it, then test repeated calls and explicit empty-list input.
mistake: Using truthiness to replace every empty caller-owned list.

q: Why use a generator to read a large log file, and what limitation must callers know?
a: Yield records lazily to bound memory. A generator is consumed as it is iterated and is not automatically reusable.
explanation: Keep the file open for the duration of iteration and close it reliably. Avoid list(...) in the caller if streaming is required. Repeated traversal needs a new iterator or stored results.
mistake: Calling a generator lazy while immediately materializing everything.

q: An async endpoint freezes other requests while calling a synchronous client. Why?
a: Blocking work still blocks the event-loop thread inside async def. Use an async client or offload suitable blocking I/O.
explanation: Use asyncio.to_thread for appropriate blocking I/O and bound concurrency. CPU-heavy Python often needs processes or native code, depending on the interpreter and workload. Preserve timeouts and cancellation.
mistake: Assuming async def makes synchronous calls nonblocking.

q: Process a huge iterable in fixed-size batches without loading it all.
a: Consume at most a batch at a time using iterator operations; explicitly handle the final partial batch.
explanation: Keep memory proportional to batch size, validate a positive size, and test empty input and exact boundaries. Choose batch size using throughput, downstream limits, and retry cost.
mistake: Slicing a prebuilt list and calling the result streaming.

q: Several independent remote lookups feed one Python response. How do you manage their lifetime?
a: Use a bounded task group and a request deadline. Specify whether one failure cancels the group or produces a partial response.
explanation: TaskGroup is available in Python 3.11+. Clean up in finally and normally propagate cancellation. Avoid orphan tasks, unbounded fan-out, and hiding all failures in empty results.
mistake: Swallowing cancellation and leaving background work running.

q: A Python ingestion worker has steadily increasing memory. How would you diagnose it?
a: Measure retained objects and allocation trends; check queues, caches, references, and whether streaming code materializes data.
explanation: Reproduce with a bounded input and compare snapshots. Distinguish expected cache growth from unbounded retention. Add queue limits and verify steady-state memory over a sustained run.
mistake: Calling garbage collection repeatedly without finding retained references.

q: Design a resumable Python ETL job that may crash after writing a batch.
a: Use durable checkpoints and idempotent or transactionally coordinated writes so replay cannot duplicate results.
explanation: Checkpoint progress only after output is durable, or commit both together when possible. Track input versions, rejected records, and schema changes. Test a crash on both sides of each commit.
mistake: Saving the checkpoint before the output is committed.
